Glossary

    Questions · IGL

    Words: 2768

    Fifty questions on decisions, not syntax. The right answer here almost always names conditions and costs rather than a command name.

    Key idea of this page #

    At this level, interviewers do not ask what syntax you recall, but what trade-offs you evaluate and what price you pay for each decision. Saying “I would write a script” is almost always weaker than “first I determine whether this is an action or a desired state.” The fifty questions are grouped into five areas: when Bash is appropriate at all; what contract a script declares when it becomes an automated tool; how it tolerates retries and sudden interruption; what bounds its worst-case blast radius; and how it lives and gets retired in production. The final group is the most frequently neglected, yet it is precisely where engineers who have managed production legacy are distinguished from those who have only written fresh greenfield code.

    Applicability decisions (1–10) #

    1. By what criteria do you decide that a task is not suited for Bash?
      Data structures beyond flat lists, floating-point arithmetic, structured error recovery, concurrency requiring inter-task communication, or logic exceeding three hundred lines.
      Why this gets asked: tests for concrete technical criteria rather than personal taste.
    2. When is a script the right choice even though a mature tool already exists?
      When the task is strictly one-off, when deploying the tool introduces prohibitive bootstrapping friction, or when running in a bare environment where nothing else is installed yet.
      Why this gets asked: checks whether you swing to the opposite dogmatic extreme.
    3. How does an action-oriented problem differ from a state-oriented problem?
      An action executes once and finishes; state must be continuously maintained, reconciled against desired state, and tracked. Managing state is not a problem for a script.
      Why this gets asked: fundamental boundary separating Bash from Terraform and configuration management.
    4. How do you respond to a request to “write a quick script that monitors and fixes things”?
      Point out that this describes a state control reconciliation loop, which already has mature solutions; a script here will simply devolve into a poorly implemented Terraform or Kubernetes controller.
      Why this gets asked: evaluates your ability to reframe problems rather than blindly implementing them.
    5. How do you assess the total cost of ownership of a shell script?
      By the number of engineers who will have to read and maintain it, the frequency of required modifications, and the blast radius of failure - not by line count.
      Why this gets asked: reflects economic and lifecycle engineering thinking.
    6. When is rewriting a functioning script an engineering mistake?
      When it is small, stable, and well-understood: maintenance overhead scales with complexity and churn, not programming language.
      Why this gets asked: tests whether you succumb to rewriting out of dogma or aesthetic bias.
    7. How do you choose between Make and a sequential shell script?
      Choose Make when dealing with dependency directed acyclic graphs and incremental execution; choose a script when execution steps are strictly linear.
      Why this gets asked: common antipattern is adopting Makefiles purely as command task runners without dependency semantics.
    8. When should logic be extracted from CI workflow YAML into repository scripts?
      As soon as it cannot be reproduced and debugged locally using the exact same command: this is an absolute requirement for reproducibility.
      Why this gets asked: evaluates understanding of the boundary between pipeline orchestration and application code.
    9. What do you do when identical shell logic is copy-pasted across three CI pipelines?
      Extract it into a shared, versioned script, container image, or reusable CI action; duplicating logic guarantees three diverging implementations within six months.
      Why this gets asked: tests discipline against code duplication at the infrastructure tier.
    10. How do you decide between authoring an in-house tool versus adopting an existing solution?
      By comparing ongoing maintenance costs and the organizational cost of the author departing the team, rather than initial implementation hours.
      Why this gets asked: tests long-term architectural planning horizons.

    Contract and compatibility (11–20) #

    1. What constitutes the contract of a script intended for machine invocation?
      Standard stream allocation (stdout for data, stderr for diagnostics), explicit exit code semantics, structured machine-readable output formats, a dry-run flag, and documented backward compatibility guarantees.
      Why this gets asked: tests whether you treat scripts as formal software interfaces.
    2. How do you distinguish “not found” from “broken execution” in exit codes?
      Use distinct exit codes: a predictable negative result returns one code (e.g., 1), while an internal failure returns another (e.g., 2); callers must handle these cases differently.
      Why this gets asked: demonstrates designing for the upstream caller rather than immediate convenience.
    3. Why should a script provide a --json flag if human output can already be parsed with awk/grep?
      So human-facing diagnostic text can evolve freely without breaking automation; without this separation, every log tweak becomes a breaking change.
      Why this gets asked: foundational API and interface stability principle.
    4. What constitutes a breaking change in an automation script?
      Changing exit code meanings, altering stdout formatting, renaming flags or environment variables, and modifying default behavior - anything downstream callers depend upon.
      Why this gets asked: evaluates understanding of backward compatibility contracts.
    5. How do you introduce new behavior without breaking existing consumers?
      Introduce a new opt-in flag with a safe default, issue deprecation warnings to stderr announcing future default changes with a target date, and only switch defaults in a subsequent major release.
      Why this gets asked: demonstrates experience with non-disruptive interface evolution.
    6. Why should a utility script support --version?
      To allow callers to verify compatibility requirements and ensure that incident issue reports are unambiguously reproducible. Implementing --version costs trivial effort.
      Why this gets asked: a small polish detail that distinguishes a maintained tool from a throwaway file.
    7. Why should --dry-run be designed into the architecture from the start rather than retrofitted?
      Retrofitted dry-run modes frequently miss dangerous conditional branches; wrapping every mutating command structurally ensures comprehensive coverage. However, wrappers do not catch redirections: run cmd > file truncates the file even in dry-run mode because the shell performs redirection before the wrapper executes. File writes must be moved inside the invoked command.
      Why this gets asked: checks whether testability is an upfront architectural concern - and whether you know shell redirection semantics.
    8. How do you document a script intended to serve as a shared engineering tool?
      A built-in --help flag and concise header comments; external wiki pages and tickets rot far faster than code.
      Why this gets asked: pragmatic utility outweighs exhaustive documentation.
    9. How do you guarantee identical behavior locally and in CI runners?
      Run the exact same command inside the exact same container image environment; diverging dependencies erode trust in test suites.
      Why this gets asked: addresses the primary root cause of “works on my machine” syndrome.
    10. Why does a shared common.sh library sourced across a dozen repositories become an architectural trap?
      Bash lacks namespaces and package versioning: source pollutes caller scopes with global variables and unintended set options, while modifying the shared library instantly destabilizes every consumer. Shared logic should be distributed as versioned container images, packaged CLIs, or CI actions.
      Why this gets asked: architectural question regarding shared code in languages without package managers.

    Reliability and idempotence (21–30) #

    1. What is idempotence in the context of shell scripting?
      Executing the script repeatedly yields the same system state without introducing errors, since retries are inevitable in distributed systems.
      Why this gets asked: central property of robust infrastructure automation.
    2. How do you make a non-idempotent operation safe for retries?
      Introduce an idempotency key or operation identifier, executing the mutation only if that key is absent from the state ledger or journal.
      Why this gets asked: evaluates practical mechanism design rather than memorized terminology.
    3. Why is a “check then act” pattern not atomic?
      Between the check and the mutation, a concurrent process can modify the state (TOCTOU race condition); you must use atomic primitives or explicit locking.
      Why this gets asked: classic concurrency race condition question at the systems level.
    4. How do you bound the total execution time of an entire script rather than individual commands?
      Rely on external orchestrator or CI job timeouts, complemented by per-operation timeouts; a single timeout command on child processes is insufficient.
      Why this gets asked: reflects the principle that a hanging task is far worse than a failing task.
    5. Why is an unbounded polling loop a defect rather than defensive programming?
      It converts an operational failure into an indefinite hang: resources remain locked until timeout, and alerting signals arrive delayed and obscured.
      Why this gets asked: probes your attitude toward failure modes and timeout handling.
    6. How do you design a script that can be safely terminated midway through execution?
      Decouple preparation from activation: stage all changes in temporary directories, then swap or activate state in a single atomic step (e.g., ln -sfn or mv -T).
      Why this gets asked: foundation of zero-downtime atomic deployments.
    7. What strategy do you use if a script must execute across heterogeneous Linux distributions?
      Define an explicit baseline of prerequisite capabilities and validate them upfront, rather than blindly assuming utility availability or flag parity.
      Why this gets asked: portability as an intentional design decision rather than accidental luck.
    8. How do you test shell code?
      Statically via shellcheck; functionally using bats or containerized ephemeral test runs against synthetic data; and mandatorily via --dry-run modes.
      Why this gets asked: verifies whether testing is an ingrained engineering discipline for shell code.
    9. Should a twenty-line script be covered by automated tests?
      Usually not: static analysis and a dry-run flag suffice. Automated test suites are justified when logic contains branching conditionals and high failure cost.
      Why this gets asked: evaluates engineering proportionality against dogmatic testing.
    10. How do you recognize when a monolithic script should be decomposed?
      When distinct subcomponents change for different business reasons or are invoked by different consumers; line count alone is a secondary indicator.
      Why this gets asked: classic single responsibility principle applied to systems scripting.

    Security and blast radius (31–40) #

    1. What is a script’s blast radius and how do you constrain it?
      The maximum damage possible during failure; constrained by scoping allowed target paths via strict allowlists and limiting the volume of mutations per run.
      Why this gets asked: tests worst-case architectural risk modeling.
    2. Why are synchronized retries across hundreds of nodes dangerous during external service degradation?
      Simultaneous retries hammer the recovering service, triggering a thundering herd failure. Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and apply randomized start delays to cron jobs (RandomizedDelaySec in systemd timers).
      Why this gets asked: evaluates single-node blast radius multiplied across an entire fleet.
    3. What must be strictly enforced during shell code reviews versus left to personal preference?
      Enforce what machines catch (shellcheck with no global suppressions), exit codes, scope constraints on destructive operations, and retry semantics. Leave formatting to shfmt. Debating formatting during review wastes team bandwidth.
      Why this gets asked: evaluates your ability to build engineering review processes.
    4. Why is curl … | bash considered an antipattern?
      Code executes uninspected, and executes incrementally: the shell interprets lines as chunks arrive over the socket, so a network disruption can leave half the script executed and truncate a command into an unintended operation. Without pipefail, download failures are completely ignored.
      Why this gets asked: combines supply chain trust analysis with deep pipeline stream mechanics.
    5. Which operations should never be delegated to autonomous AI agents without human confirmation?
      Deletions, privilege escalation, downloading and executing network binaries, and rewriting shared VCS history - actions that are irreversible or disrupt others.
      Why this gets asked: timely topic regarding safe autonomous operational boundaries.
    6. How do you minimize the privilege envelope of a running script?
      Run under dedicated unprivileged service accounts, grant fine-grained sudo command permissions rather than root shells, and restrict accessible filesystem trees.
      Why this gets asked: practical application of the principle of least privilege.
    7. How do you protect a script downloading binary assets from tampering?
      Pin exact release versions and verify cryptographic checksums recorded in the source repository prior to execution. Relying on “latest release” is trusting an unverified external third party.
      Why this gets asked: essential software supply chain security hygiene.
    8. What must you do if a secret is accidentally committed to a repository or printed to CI logs?
      Immediately treat the secret as compromised and revoke/rotate it; scrubbing git history or deleting log lines does not undo potential exposure.
      Why this gets asked: evaluates standard security incident response discipline.
    9. How do you ensure auditability for script actions?
      Emit structured logs to stderr including execution run IDs, and stream them to centralized log aggregation infrastructure.
      Why this gets asked: evaluates operational traceability and compliance.
    10. Why does an allowlist of command names fail to secure an agent or user environment?
      Innocuous-looking utilities can execute arbitrary code or destroy data: find -delete, tar --checkpoint-action, git -c core.pager=…, env, or any language runtime. Real security boundaries require sandbox isolation and inspecting full argument vectors.
      Why this gets asked: examines where true system security boundaries exist.

    Operations and lifecycle (41–50) #

    1. What must a script report about itself in production?
      Outcome, exit code, elapsed duration, and volume of processed work - the baseline metrics needed to graph trends and detect gradual degradation.
      Why this gets asked: tests whether you design with observability in mind.
    2. Why is key-value formatted logging preferred over unformatted prose?
      It is parsed effortlessly by log collectors without complex regular expressions and does not break when human-facing wording is modified.
      Why this gets asked: practical systems logging discipline.
    3. How do you distinguish system degradation from outright failure in script telemetry?
      Through duration and volume: outright failure is signaled by exit code, while degradation is only visible through trending increases in runtime or drops in throughput.
      Why this gets asked: evaluates understanding of the difference between monitoring metrics and discrete alerts.
    4. How do you decommission a legacy script in production?
      Through a proxy phase: log deprecation notices with explicit sunset dates to stderr and forward calls to the new tool until upstream callers disappear from logs.
      Why this gets asked: the most frequently ignored phase of software lifecycle management.
    5. How do you safely replace a mission-critical 1000-line legacy script with a dedicated service or tool without downtime?
      Incrementally: extract isolated high-complexity sections into standalone utilities called from the legacy script, run the new service in parallel shadow mode, compare outputs, and cut over only after zero discrepancies are verified.
      Why this gets asked: checks experience with safe migration patterns avoiding big-bang cutovers.
    6. How do you identify all upstream consumers invoking your script?
      Log incoming invocations along with caller environment and process metadata to central logging; repository code searches frequently miss ad-hoc crons and dynamic callers.
      Why this gets asked: pragmatic operational telemetry over theoretical guesswork.
    7. How do you safely approach a massive legacy script that everyone is terrified to touch?
      Surround it with automated safety nets first: enable shellcheck, add a dry-run mode, establish integration regression tests, and only then begin refactoring.
      Why this gets asked: classic interview question on managing legacy technical debt.
    8. How do you transfer ownership of an automation script to another team?
      Through --help output, header documentation, and an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) explaining why it exists and when it should be retired.
      Why this gets asked: assesses whether documentation is treated as an integral deliverable.
    9. How do you prevent a “one-off temporary script” from surviving for five years?
      Assign an explicit owner, set an expiration date in the header, place it in an audited location, and on its first reuse make an explicit decision: retire it or promote it to a maintained tool. Temporary scripts become critical legacy not by design, but because nobody made the decision not to.
      Why this gets asked: evaluates handling of temporary operational work that often becomes technical debt.
    10. What indicator tells you that automation should not be built at all?
      The task occurs rarely, takes only minutes, and demands human contextual judgment at every step: automating it costs far more than doing the manual work.
      Why this gets asked: tests whether you know when NOT to build software.

    Artifacts: what you take away from this page #

    Reading >> Your life quantum · Dignity partnership with AI · Rewiring your neural network

    Fifty architectural decisions with explicit trade-offs. Your time was well spent if you began answering technical questions with preconditions: “if the task manages state, then...”, “if there is more than one caller, then...”. That is the essence of rewiring your neural network: an answer stops being an arbitrary technology choice and becomes an accountable architectural decision.

    1. Applicability criteria: action versus state, and total cost of ownership.
    2. Tool contracts and principles of unbroken backward compatibility.
    3. Idempotence, race conditions, and interruptions as intentional design targets.
    4. Blast radius, allowlists, and least privilege - designing from the worst case.
    5. Observability and decommissioning with explicit sunset dates and proxying phases.
